verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: `rand.Int63n(int64(MaxJitter))` panics with "invalid argument to Int63n" whenever MaxJitter is <= 0, and the newly added exported constant MaxJitter has no positivity guard. WHY: a zero or negative MaxJitter (e.g. a later config/env override or a test setting it to 0 to disable jitter) crashes the worker process inside Dispatcher.Tick every time a job fails. HOW: guard the jitter, e.g. `var jitter time.Duration; if MaxJitter > 0 { jitter = time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(MaxJitter))) }`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: REFUTED. MaxJitter is a package-level const with a fixed value of 10 * time.Second (line 11) and is referenced only at line 29. Go constants cannot be overridden at runtime by config/env, and there are no other usages (grep shows only definition and single use). No test or caller can set MaxJitter to 0/negative. rand.Int63n(int64(10*time.Second)) is always called with a positive argument, so the claimed panic is impossible. The speculative 'later config/env override' scenario cannot occur with a const, and the finding supplies no concrete code path where MaxJitter is non-positive.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The new exponential backoff `BaseDelay * time.Duration(1<<job.Attempts)` is only capped by the `job.Attempts >= MaxAttempts` guard, but that guard is unreachable from the only caller: dispatch.go:28-29 does `job.Attempts++` before calling `nextAttemptAt(job, now)`, so the first failure passes Attempts=1 and the guard needs Attempts>=5. WHY: since jobs that hit the cap keep being returned by Due (the capped branch still returns `now`), Attempts keeps incrementing and `1<<job.Attempts` overflows `time.Duration` (1<<63 wraps negative), producing a negative backoff so `now.Add(backoff + jitter)` lands in the past and the job is due again on the very next tick — backoff silently stops working instead of slowing the job down. HOW: cap the shift, e.g. `if job.Attempts >= MaxAttempts { return now.Add(time.Hour) }` (fixing the cap for real) and clamp the exponent: `shift := job.Attempts; if shift > 10 { shift = 10 }`, then `backoff := BaseDelay * time.Duration(1<<shift)`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Verified: dispatch.go:28 does `job.Attempts++` before calling nextAttemptAt, so the first failure passes Attempts=1. The `job.Attempts >= MaxAttempts` (5) guard is only reached after 5 increments, and once reached it returns `now` (not a future time), so the job remains Due on every tick and Attempts keeps incrementing. With `time.Duration(1<<job.Attempts)`, at Attempts>=63 the shift overflows int64 and wraps negative, producing a negative backoff so `now.Add(backoff+jitter)` can land in the past — backoff silently breaks. The code matches the claim exactly; the overflow path is reachable because the capped branch keeps re-scheduling the same job at `now`. Note: the PreviousReviewDecision round-a-P28-retry-cap-next-run-now already raised the cap-never-stops-the-job problem (the retry cap failing to stop a failing job). The present finding's core failure — the same job being re-run indefinitely because the cap branch returns `now` — is the same underlying failure already raised by that entry, so it overlaps with an existing PR comment. However, the specific new mechanism claimed here (integer shift overflow at 1<<Attempts producing a negative backoff that lands in the past) is a distinct consequence not described by that entry. Since the rule says to drop only on refutation, and the technical claim itself is factually correct and reachable, I keep it; but flag that it substantially restates the already-posted retry-cap finding.

HOW: run both fields through stripInlineMarkup (which removes `<...>` tokens) before interpolating: `text: `${stripInlineMarkup(m.authorName)} mentioned you: ${stripInlineMarkup(m.body)}\n<${m.threadUrl}|Open the thread>``.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Confirmed: mentionChat (mentions.ts:22) interpolates m.authorName and m.body raw into the ChatClient `text` field, while clients.ts:6-7 documents that text is chat markup where <url|label> renders a link and <!channel> pings everyone. sanitize.ts's stripInlineMarkup exists and its comment states every outbound sink should pass user text through it; mentionEmail was already fixed (lines 15-16) but mentionChat was not. This is a distinct sink/operation from PreviousDecision #1 (which addressed email HTML/subject phishing), so it is a different problem, not a repeat. Claim's root cause, path, and fix all hold.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: mentionInbox interpolates m.authorName and m.body directly into the `html` field passed to inbox.add, with no call to stripInlineMarkup, even though Mention.authorName/body are comment and display-name user input and sanitize.ts documents that every outbound sink sanitizes first. WHY: InboxStore's contract says `html` is rendered as is in the web app's notification inbox, so a commenter can store arbitrary markup (e.g. `` or a styled fake login form) that executes/renders inside our own origin for the mentioned user — a stored XSS/HTML-injection vector in the authenticated app. HOW: sanitize both fields before embedding: `html: `${stripInlineMarkup(m.authorName)} mentioned you: ${stripInlineMarkup(m.body)}``.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Confirmed: line 28 interpolates m.authorName and m.body directly into the `html` field with no stripInlineMarkup, while the sibling sink mentionEmail (lines 15-16) does sanitize. sanitize.ts documents that every outbound sink sanitizes, and clients.ts confirms InboxStore renders `html` as-is in the web app, so attacker-controlled comment/display-name markup (e.g. onerror img) is a stored HTML-injection/XSS into our own origin. The prior decision (round-a-P37-markup-strip-new-sinks) addressed only mentionEmail's subject/body — a separate sink/operation. Same class of bug in a distinct outbound sink is a different problem, not a repeat.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: The new mentionChat and mentionInbox sinks interpolate the raw user-controlled m.authorName and m.body into chat text and inbox HTML without passing them through stripInlineMarkup, unlike mentionEmail which sanitizes both. WHY: A comment body such as `Reset password` renders as a live link in the chat client and in the web inbox, and chat markup like `` pings the entire channel — a ready phishing/abuse vector from our own notification surface, exactly the class of issue sanitize.ts:1-3 documents as covered by 'every outbound sink'. HOW: Import stripInlineMarkup (already imported in this file) and wrap the user text in both new sinks, e.g. `${stripInlineMarkup(m.authorName)} mentioned you: ${stripInlineMarkup(m.body)}` and `${stripInlineMarkup(m.authorName)} mentioned you: ${stripInlineMarkup(m.body)}`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Code confirms the claim: mentionEmail (lines 15-16) wraps both m.authorName and m.body in stripInlineMarkup, but mentionChat (line 22) and mentionInbox (line 28) interpolate the raw user-controlled values. sanitize.ts documents that every outbound sink must sanitize, and the regex strips HTML tags and chat markup. The previous review decision (round-a-P37) addressed only the email sink; chat and inbox are separate sinks and distinct operations, so this is not a repeat of that entry. Keep.

verificationEvidence.claim: WHAT: mentionChat interpolates the raw user-controlled m.authorName and m.body into the chat message text, which ChatClient.post documents as interpreting chat markup (`<url|label>` renders a link, `<!channel>` pings everyone). WHY: any commenter can put `<!channel>` in a mention body to ping every member of the channel, or `<https://evil.example|Reset password>` to render a live phishing link in a message from our bot. HOW: wrap both interpolations in stripInlineMarkup, as mentionEmail already does: `${stripInlineMarkup(m.authorName)} mentioned you: ${stripInlineMarkup(m.body)}\n<${m.threadUrl}|Open the thread>`.
verificationEvidence.rationale: Confirmed: mentionChat (src/notifications/mentions.ts:22) interpolates raw m.authorName and m.body into chat text, while ChatClient.post (clients.ts:6-7) explicitly documents that `text` interprets chat markup (<url|label>, <!channel>). The file already imports stripInlineMarkup and mentionEmail (lines 15-16) applies it, but the chat path does not — so a commenter can inject <!channel> or a phishing link rendered by our bot. This is a distinct sink from the previously-decided mentionEmail issue (round-a-P37 was about the email subject/HTML; this is the chat post path), so it is not a repeat. The claim's root cause, code path, and fix are accurate.
